titulo: Module 07 — Exam: multi-agent orchestration, decomposition, multi-pass review, and sessions

questoes.pergunta: A multi-agent research system receives: "overview of renewable energy in Brazil". The coordinator creates subtasks on residential solar panels, solar power plants, and solar energy incentives. The report comes out well written and well supported, but it ignores wind, hydroelectric, and biomass. The logs show that each subagent did exactly what it was given. What is the best fix?
opcoes: Improve the search subagents' prompt so they bring back more diverse sources
Fix the coordinator's decomposition to cover the entire scope and add an explicit coverage check before synthesis
Add a reviewer subagent at the end that rewrites the report with broader coverage
Switch the coordinator's model to one with a larger context window
questoes.explicacao: Overly narrow decomposition is a coordinator defect. The subagents did what they were given; the fix is to decompose more broadly and check coverage.
feedbacks: Targets the component that worked: the subagents searched for exactly what they were asked to.
Correct. The gap originates in the decomposition.
A reviewer at the end has no material on wind and hydroelectric to include: none of that was researched. It treats the symptom too late.
The context window has nothing to do with the scope of the decomposition.

questoes.pergunta: In the same research system, after 20 turns discussing with the user that the focus is "Latin American logistics startups with a Series A round in 2025", the coordinator delegates: "Research the companies we discussed and bring back the funding data." The subagent comes back with generic data on large U.S. logistics companies. What is the cause and the fix?
opcoes: The subagent uses a weaker model; use the same model as the coordinator
A better search tool is missing; integrate a startup database
The subagent should have asked for clarification; instruct it to always ask when in doubt
The subagent has an isolated context and did not see the conversation; the delegation must explicitly include region, stage, year, criteria, and output format
questoes.explicacao: Subagents do not inherit the coordinator's history. "The companies we discussed" doesn't exist for the subagent: everything goes explicitly into the delegation prompt.
feedbacks: Even the best model can't guess what it never received.
The tool isn't the problem: the subagent doesn't even know what to look for.
Shifts to the subagent work that belongs to the coordinator and adds unnecessary round trips; the direct fix is to delegate with full context.
Correct.

questoes.pergunta: The coordinator of a research system needs to query four independent sources for each question. Metrics show latency equal to the sum of the four queries. The logs reveal one `Agent` call per coordinator turn. What is the simplest fix?
opcoes: Instruct the coordinator to emit the four `Agent` calls in the same response when the subtasks are independent
Replace the subagents with a single agent that has all the tools for the four sources
Increase the maximum subagent concurrency setting
Move each source to a separate process orchestrated by an external queue
questoes.explicacao: Subagent parallelism = multiple `Agent` `tool_use` blocks in the same response. One per turn is sequential by construction.
feedbacks: Correct.
Crams too many tools into one agent and doesn't solve the parallelism.
The limit isn't being hit: the coordinator emits one subagent at a time.
New infrastructure for something the protocol itself already solves: violates the simplest fix.

questoes.pergunta: To "gain speed", an engineer proposes that the analysis subagent send questions directly to the search subagent, without going through the coordinator. What is the best assessment?
opcoes: Good idea, as long as the direct messages are logged
Good idea, because it reduces the coordinator's context load
Reject it: in hub-and-spoke the coordinator routes all communication, which preserves observability, error handling, and coverage control
Reject it, because subagents cannot call tools
questoes.explicacao: Direct communication between subagents is an anti-pattern: it takes away the coordinator's view of the whole, its error handling, and its gap detection.
feedbacks: Logging doesn't give the coordinator back control over error handling or the ability to assess gaps.
Tempting, but the coordinator loses exactly the view it needs to aggregate and re-delegate.
Correct.
Subagents use tools normally; the problem is the communication topology.

questoes.pergunta: An internal research assistant is expensive: even simple factual questions ("when was company X founded?") go through web search, academic search, trend analysis, and review. The quality of the answers to complex questions is good. What should change?
opcoes: Create a separate classifier, trained to decide the route for each question
Have the coordinator evaluate each query and invoke only the subagents needed
Reduce the `max_tokens` of all subagents
Remove academic search and review from all queries
questoes.explicacao: Invoking only what the query needs is the coordinator's job; it is the simplest fix and preserves the quality of the complex queries.
feedbacks: More complex than necessary: the coordinator can already decide this with clear criteria.
Correct.
Cuts answers off midway without reducing the number of subagents invoked.
Hurts the complex queries, which currently work well.

questoes.pergunta: In the final report of a research system, a market share figure appears without a source, and two subagents had found different values (31% and 27%), but the report shows only 29%. The subagents return prose paragraphs. What is the best change?
opcoes: Instruct the coordinator to always pick the value from the most recent source
Ask the synthesizer to cite the sources at the end of the report
Add a verifier subagent that redoes all the searches
Have the subagents return structured output separating content from metadata (claim, evidence, source, date), and have the synthesis record the conflicting values with their sources
questoes.explicacao: Structured handoff (content + metadata) preserves attribution. A conflict between sources should be annotated, not resolved by averaging or by silent selection.
feedbacks: Choosing silently hides the conflict, and the most recent source may be measuring something else.
Without metadata coming from the subagents, the synthesizer has no way of knowing where each number came from.
Redoing searches doesn't fix the format that loses attribution; it's double the cost.
Correct.

questoes.pergunta: After the first round, the research coordinator evaluates the synthesis and notices that the regulatory perspective is missing and that a 2023 data point needs updating. What is the most appropriate next step?
opcoes: Launch a second round targeted only at those gaps, then synthesize
Rerun all the subagents with the same prompts
Deliver the report with a note saying it may be incomplete
Ask the user to research the regulatory part
questoes.explicacao: Iterative refinement: evaluate → identify gaps → targeted 2nd round → synthesize.
feedbacks: Correct.
Repeats work already done and doesn't target the gaps.
Giving up on identifiable, fixable gaps is not the expected behavior of the coordinator.
Shifts to the user work that the system can do.

questoes.pergunta: A company uses Claude Code in CI to review PRs. On PRs with more than 30 files, the review flags superficial issues, enforces a standard in some files and ignores it in others, and missed a signature change that broke three callers in other modules. What is the best restructuring?
opcoes: Use a model with a larger context window so the whole PR fits
Run the same review three times and consolidate by voting
Pass 1 per file, with the same prompt for all; pass 2 for integration, with a separate prompt, receiving the pass 1 findings to analyze contracts and flow between modules
Ask the author to split every PR into PRs of at most 5 files
questoes.explicacao: Multi-pass review solves attention dilution (local pass), inconsistency (same prompt per file), and cross-file bugs (integration pass).
feedbacks: Fitting in the window doesn't solve attention dilution in a single pass.
Voting across reviews that suffer from the same problem doesn't create the integration pass.
Correct.
A process constraint that doesn't solve the tool's problem and isn't always feasible.

questoes.pergunta: A team uses a Claude Code session to implement a feature and, at the end, in the same session, asks: "now critically review your code". The review almost never finds problems, but QA finds several. What is the most likely cause and the best fix?
opcoes: The review prompt is weak; ask the model to be "extremely rigorous"
Reasoning-context bias: whoever generated it doesn't question its own decisions. Review in an independent session that sees only the code
Lack of time; run the review with maximum `effort` in the same session
Fork the session to review, taking advantage of the cache
questoes.explicacao: Self-review in the same session is an anti-pattern. An independent instance evaluates the artifact without the reasoning that justified it.
feedbacks: An instruction doesn't remove the biased context; the model remains "convinced" by its own reasoning.
Correct.
More effort in the same context keeps the bias.
The fork inherits the entire conversation, including the biased reasoning. Cheap, but not independent.

questoes.pergunta: You are designing the multi-pass review pipeline for large PRs in CI. Which decisions are correct? (Choose TWO.)
opcoes: Use, in pass 2, the same session that generated the code, because it knows the intentions
Apply the same review prompt to each file in pass 1, to keep the criteria consistent
Skip pass 1 when the PR fits in the context window
Let each file use a different prompt, adapted by the model itself
Pass the pass 1 findings to pass 2, focusing on contracts, data flow, and errors across modules
questoes.explicacao: Pass 1: per file, consistent prompt. Pass 2: separate integration prompt, fed by the pass 1 findings. All in a session independent from the one that generated the code.
feedbacks: Reintroduces reasoning-context bias.
Correct.
Fitting in the window doesn't eliminate attention dilution.
Different prompts produce exactly the inconsistency you want to avoid.
Correct.

questoes.pergunta: Yesterday, a Claude Code session mapped the billing module and started a refactoring plan. Overnight, another developer merged a change that reorganized half of that module's files. How should you continue?
opcoes: Use `--resume` and follow the plan normally
Use `--resume` with `--fork-session` to get a new ID
Use `--continue`, which reloads the files automatically
Start a new session with a structured summary of what was decided, letting Claude reread the current state of the module
questoes.explicacao: When files have changed, the tool results in the history are stale and the model trusts them. Start a new session with a summary (or, if resuming, state explicitly what changed).
feedbacks: The history holds the old file contents; Claude would edit based on code that no longer exists.
A new ID doesn't refresh the stale results inherited from the base.
`--continue` resumes the most recent session with the same history; it doesn't reread anything automatically.
Correct.

questoes.pergunta: A Claude Code session spent an hour analyzing a legacy service. The tech lead wants to compare two modernization strategies (strangler fig vs. rewrite) based on that analysis, without the experiments of one contaminating the other. What is the best approach?
opcoes: Resume the session twice with `--resume` and `--fork-session`, one per strategy
Try one strategy, undo it with git, and try the other in the same session
Open two new sessions and repeat the analysis in each one
Ask Claude, in the same session, to "forget" the first strategy before the second
questoes.explicacao: `--fork-session` creates branches with new IDs from the common base: it reuses the analysis without contamination between the branches.
feedbacks: Correct.
Undoing the files doesn't remove the decisions and results of the first attempt from the history.
Works, but throws away an hour of valid analysis.
Asking it to forget doesn't remove anything from the context.

questoes.pergunta: A developer needs to resume a bug investigation session because most of the context is still valid, but since then the developer has personally changed two configuration files. What is the correct way to resume?
opcoes: Resume and mention nothing; Claude will notice the changes on its own
Resume and ask Claude to reread the entire repository
Resume and state explicitly what changed (which files and how), asking Claude to reread those two before continuing
Delete the session's tool result history before resuming
questoes.explicacao: When resuming after changes, say what changed: the stale results remain in the history and the model trusts them.
feedbacks: Claude has no way of knowing; the old results look valid.
Overkill: wastes context rereading what didn't change.
Correct.
Editing the history is risky and unnecessary; just report the change.

questoes.pergunta: A data extraction company always processes contracts the same way: extract parties and dates, classify risk clauses, validate required fields, and generate a summary. A proposal suggests an orchestrator agent that dynamically decides the steps. What is the best recommendation?
opcoes: Approve the orchestrator, since it adapts to future contracts
Prompt chaining with the fixed steps and validation gates between them
Parallelization via voting at every step
A single agent with all the tools, with no defined steps
questoes.explicacao: Fixed, known steps → prompt chaining. Dynamic decomposition would bring cost and unpredictability with no gain.
feedbacks: Hypothetical flexibility doesn't justify present complexity; it violates "start simple".
Correct.
Voting repeats the same task for consensus; here the steps are different and sequential.
Gives up predictability in a process that is predictable.

questoes.pergunta: A product team wants to investigate why checkout conversion dropped 12% in the last week. Possible causes range from a frontend deploy to a change in the payment gateway or a marketing campaign, and each discovery changes where to look next. Which decomposition strategy is the most appropriate?
opcoes: Prompt chaining with five fixed steps defined in advance
Routing by cause type, chosen from the first message
Parallelization via sectioning with fixed subtasks, with no later rounds
Dynamic decomposition (orchestrator-workers), in which subtasks emerge from the discoveries
questoes.explicacao: An open-ended investigation, in which each finding changes the plan, calls for dynamic/adaptive decomposition.
feedbacks: Fixed steps ignore what the discoveries reveal.
The cause isn't known at the start; there is nothing to route.
May be useful in a first round, but fixed subtasks without adaptation don't keep up with the discoveries.
Correct.

questoes.pergunta: A support center receives 70% simple FAQ questions and 30% complex billing and technical cases. Today everything goes to the largest model with the same prompt, which is expensive and slow. Which pattern from "Building Effective Agents" solves this best?
opcoes: Routing: classify the input and send simple questions to a smaller model and complex cases to specialized flows
Evaluator-optimizer: one model generates and another evaluates each answer
Orchestrator-workers for all questions
Parallelization via voting to increase confidence
questoes.explicacao: Routing separates distinct categories and lets you direct the easy ones to smaller/cheaper models.
feedbacks: Correct.
Adds cost to every question, including the trivial ones.
Dynamic decomposition is overkill for FAQ questions.
Multiplies the cost of precisely what you want to make cheaper.

questoes.pergunta: A team translates technical documentation with clear terminology and style rules, and a second read with feedback usually improves the translation measurably. Which pattern fits best?
opcoes: Routing
Prompt chaining without gates
Evaluator-optimizer: one LLM translates, another evaluates it against the criteria and returns feedback, in a loop until it meets them
Orchestrator-workers
questoes.explicacao: Clear evaluation criteria + iterative refinement with measurable gain = evaluator-optimizer.
feedbacks: There are no distinct categories to route.
A fixed sequence without evaluation doesn't take advantage of iterative feedback.
Correct.
The subtasks aren't unpredictable; the gain comes from evaluating and refining.

questoes.pergunta: Regarding subagent spawning and context passing, which statements are correct? (Choose TWO.)
opcoes: For the coordinator to create subagents, the `Agent` tool must be among its allowed tools
The subagent automatically inherits the coordinator's entire history
In the Agent SDK, messages produced inside a subagent carry `parent_tool_use_id`, which allows attributing them to the right subagent
Subagents run in parallel when the coordinator creates them in consecutive turns
The subagent returns its entire tool call history to the coordinator, in addition to the result
questoes.explicacao: `Agent` (formerly `Task`) must be in `allowedTools`; `parent_tool_use_id` provides attribution. Context is isolated, parallelism requires the same response, and only the final result comes back.
feedbacks: Correct.
Isolated context: only the delegation prompt reaches the fresh subagent.
Correct.
Consecutive turns = sequential. Parallel requires multiple `Agent` calls in the same response.
Only the final result comes back; that is what keeps the coordinator's context clean.

questoes.pergunta: In a long Claude Code session, an architect and Claude defined dozens of constraints for a new module (patterns, dependency limits, API decisions). Now the architect wants to delegate generating a prototype that respects all these constraints, without polluting the main session with the exploratory work. What is the best option?
opcoes: A fresh subagent with the prompt "generate the prototype according to what we agreed on"
A fork, which inherits the entire conversation (with the constraints), shares the prompt cache, and returns only the final result
Build the prototype in the main session anyway
A fresh subagent and, if it gets things wrong, fix them in the main session
questoes.explicacao: When the subtask depends on much of what has already been discussed, the fork is ideal: it inherits the context, is cheaper thanks to the cache, and keeps the main session clean.
feedbacks: The fresh subagent doesn't know what was "agreed on": isolated context.
Correct.
Pollutes the main context with the exploratory work, which is what the architect wants to avoid.
Accepts a predictable failure and still pollutes the main session with the corrections.

questoes.pergunta: A startup wants an assistant that answers questions about its base of 200 help articles. The team's proposal is a system with a coordinator, a search subagent, a writing subagent, and a reviewer subagent. What are the best first steps? (Choose TWO.)
opcoes: Implement all four agents at once so there's no need to refactor later
Start with a single LLM call with retrieval over the articles and examples of good answers
Adopt a full agent framework before any prototype
Measure quality on a set of test questions and only add steps (e.g., a reviewer) if the gain shows up
Add an extra subagent for each article category
questoes.explicacao: "Building Effective Agents": start with the simplest solution (an LLM augmented with retrieval) and only add complexity when it demonstrably improves the result.
feedbacks: Premature complexity: more cost, latency, and points of failure with no proven gain.
Correct.
Frameworks abstract away prompts and responses and make debugging harder; they are not the first step.
Correct.
Multiplies agents without evidence of need.
